title: An Expectancy-Value Pop-Up Debate (Valued Within Exercise)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. describes a low-prep, roughly 20-minute pop-up debate in which students argue which core subject (math, science, social studies or ELA) is the best. The activity is designed to build expectancy-value mindsets, deepen students' grasp of Fulkersonian collaborative argument, and let them practice Palmer's PVLEGS speaking components. He lays out the lesson in three phases: preparation (PVLEGS goal-setting, a reteach of paraphrasing to cure 'silo arguments', a 100-word quickwrite, a scorekeeper and speech limits), his in-debate moves (tracking speakers on a clipboard, quick specific interruptions praising skill, modeling arguments himself), and a post-debate reflection. His closing claim is that because every student defends the value of a school subject, the debate quietly raises students' sense of school's worth without any manipulation. The piece is a concrete, replicable teaching-method write-up grounded in his larger framework of argument and academic mindsets.
points: The debate's real payload is motivational: having every student argue for the value of a subject builds the 'value' side of expectancy-value mindsets.
Reteaching paraphrasing ('Paraphrase Plus') directly targets 'silo arguments' where students speak in isolation, which is what makes pop-up debates go flat.
The teacher's in-debate job is brief, specific interruptions naming effective PVLEGS and Fulkersonian moves, plus modeling arguments himself.
A short post-debate Think-Pair-Share reflection places the onus for good discussion on students rather than the teacher.
Minimal prep and speaking limits (one to two speeches per student) make the format workable in 20 minutes for a 30-student class.
quotes: I told them in this debate, I wanted to see them build on someone else’s ideas using Paraphrase Plus.
I stand up, say what I think, and then I sit down; you stand up, say what you think in isolation from what I’ve said, and then sit down; repeat 30 more times.

Interrupting to point out effective performances of various PVLEGS components or Fulkersonian moves, especially fair paraphrasing: These interruptions are quick and specific; I want to point out examples of the kind of skill I believe we are capable of.
This reflective piece is easy to miss, but it is an important step in placing the onus for good discussions on kids, not the teacher.

I was surprised to find students all across the spectrums of ability and motivation getting passionate about subject area they chose, and my hunch is that, in both the subject area of their choice and the subject areas they heard their peers argue for, students walked out of my room that day with increased notions of the value of school.
I never try to trick students, but in a way this argument did end up tricking us all into examining the many reasons why school isn’t as pointless as so many believe.
